steps.text:
INTRODUCTION
## I-A Motivation
- aerial grasping: rapidly growing field
  - UAVs for drone delivery: food delivery, search and rescue, environmental cleaning, medical goods delivery
  - safety + efficiency of goods during delivery critical
  - our solution: soft aerial vehicle (SAV) w/ modular soft pneumatic gripper; little attention in previous studies
- soft grippers vs rigid
  - simpler control, less complexity, good force absorption
  - lightweight, controllable; dampen impact forces -> stability during grasping
  - flexibility -> wider range of object dimensions, more grasping tolerance
  - beneath SAV center of gravity; inflate/deflate to grasp securely -> better efficiency, less mission time
  - replaces rigid landing gear -> better aerial manipulation capability
  - no extra actuators, no landing gear adjustment during takeoff/landing/grasping
  - modular -> configurations for various object sizes/shapes (e.g. food packages)
## I-B Related Work
- inspired by birds: soft grippers mitigate contact forces, compensate grasping inaccuracies; morphological computation = passive mechanical components + explicit control
- tendon-actuated bio-inspired soft grippers: bending controlled via tendon
- Ramon et al.: soft landing gear, drone perches autonomously on pipes in industrial environments
  - nylon strands, modular design for gripper replacement
  - outdoor: closes around pipes; works in uncertain, windy conditions despite imperfect centering/fastening
- Fishman et al.: tendon-actuated gripper for soft drone, inspired by human fingers
  - no gripper state measurement; open-loop; unknown shapes on unknown surfaces; relies on object centroid
- tendon fabrication: tubes inside fingers for tendons; pneumatic: only air chamber per finger
- tendon gripper location constrained by motor; pneumatic more configurational flexibility (air tube); air tube quickly connects to pumps/valves
- pneumatic in aerial grasping:
  - Shtarbanov: FlowIO, wearable modular pneumatic platform; pneumatic viable in miniaturized, cost-effective UAV applications
  - Ping et al.: soft pneumatic gripper under conventional drone (like ours)
    - not focused on autonomous aerial grasping or removing rigid landing gear
    - single command: pneumatic pressure; Grasping Unit minimal impact on quadrotor dynamics
    - no extra DOF, gripper doesn't stick out -> rigid landing gear limits grasping altitude
  - Sarkar et al.: 2 DOF arm + pneumatic soft gripper under traditional UAV w/ rigid landing gear
    - extra mechanisms/control for home and pick positions
    - fixed rigid landing gear adds weight; over 3 kg total
## I-C Contribution
- SAV: aerial grasping + landing with lightweight modular soft pneumatic gripper
- feed-forward proportional controller for pressure; gripper = soft landing gear when deflated
- no extra landing gear; two configurations; streamlined system
- contributions:
  - modular connectors: less configuration/fabrication time; four fingers -> two configurations by object shape
  - dual role grasping + landing gear; deflation -> soft landing gear; no rigid gear -> lighter, more efficient flight, simpler control
  - 808 g total (with H-base gripper) grasps 217 g cylindrical plastic container mid-air; payload-to-weight ratio better than previous work

During drone delivery it is critical that the goods are kept safe and that delivery is efficient. So we want to address these concerns with a new solution, which is a soft aerial vehicle (SAV) with a modular soft pneumatic gripper. This has not had much attention in previous studies.

Soft grippers are a promising alternative to rigid grippers because their control systems are simpler, they are less complex, and they absorb force very well. steps.text:
INTRODUCTION
## I-A Motivation

Aerial grasping is a research field that is growing quickly, especially for unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) that are used for drone delivery, like food delivery, search and rescue, environmental cleaning, and medical goods delivery. During drone delivery it is critical that the goods are kept safe and that delivery is efficient. So we want to address these concerns with a new solution, which is a soft aerial vehicle (SAV) with a modular soft pneumatic gripper. This has not had much attention in previous studies.

Soft grippers are a promising alternative to rigid grippers because their control systems are simpler, they are less complex, and they absorb force very well. These lightweight and controllable mechanisms use the principles of soft robotics, and they give stability during grasping because they dampen impact forces. They are flexible, so they can handle a wider range of object dimensions, which increases grasping tolerance. The soft gripper is placed beneath the center of gravity of the SAV, and it can inflate and deflate to grasp objects securely, which improves grasping efficiency and reduces mission time. Also, if we replace the rigid landing gear with the soft gripper and use it as the landing mechanism, the SAV's capability for aerial manipulation is improved. There is no need for additional actuators, and the control system is simpler because the complicated landing gear adjustment during takeoff, landing, and grasping is not needed. In addition, the gripper has a modular design, so its configuration can be changed for various object sizes and shapes, for example the diverse shapes of food packages that are common in food delivery.

## I-B Related Work

Soft grippers are inspired by biological systems such as birds, and they have been shown to reduce contact forces and compensate for grasping inaccuracies. This is an example of morphological computation, which combines passive mechanical components with explicit control. To use these advantages, some researchers have developed a bio-inspired tendon-actuated soft gripper, since the bending of the gripper can be controlled easily by manipulating the attached tendon. For perching, Ramon et al. have designed a soft landing gear system which lets an aerial drone perch autonomously on pipes in industrial environments. It gives robust attachment using nylon strands and has a modular design so the gripper can be replaced. In outdoor experiments this soft gripper closed around pipes successfully, and the quadrotor performed well even in uncertain and windy conditions, even though the centering or fastening was not perfect. Also, Fishman et al. have developed a tendon-actuated soft gripper for a soft drone which is inspired by the dexterity of human fingers. Their approach does not need gripper state measurement. The soft gripper is operated open-loop to grasp objects of unknown shape on unknown surfaces, and it relies on the centroid of the objects.

To fabricate the tendon-actuated soft gripper, tubes have to be inserted inside the soft fingers so that the tendons can pass through. A pneumatic soft gripper, on the other hand, only needs a sufficient air chamber in each soft finger for bending. Also, where the tendon-actuated gripper can be placed is constrained by the position of the motor that drives it. Soft pneumatic grippers have more configurational flexibility because the air tube is flexible, and the air tube can quickly connect the pneumatic soft gripper with the pumps and valves. Related work has also looked at pneumatic soft systems for aerial grasping. Shtarbanov developed FlowIO, which is a wearable and modular pneumatic platform for soft robotics, and it showed that pneumatic systems are viable in miniaturized applications that are cost-effective for UAVs doing aerial grasping. Ping et al. put a soft pneumatic gripper under a conventional drone, which is similar to our design. But they do not focus explicitly on autonomous aerial grasping tasks or on removing the need for additional rigid landing gear. Their soft gripper is controlled by a single command, which is pneumatic pressure. They say that installing the whole Grasping Unit has minimal impact on the dynamics of the quadrotor. Their soft gripper does not stick out by adding extra degrees of freedom (DOF) to help grasping, so the rigid landing gear of their UAV limits the grasping altitude. Another work installs a 2 DOF robot arm with a pneumatic soft gripper under a traditional UAV that has rigid landing gear. Compared to our SAV, the work of Sarkar et al. needs extra mechanisms and control algorithms to make sure the manipulator can reach its home and pick positions. Their fixed, rigid landing gear also adds to the net weight of the UAV, which is over 3 kg in total.

## I-C Contribution

The SAV we propose is a significant advancement, and it can do aerial grasping and landing with a lightweight modular soft pneumatic gripper. The pneumatic soft gripper has a feed-forward proportional controller to regulate pressure precisely, and when it is deflated it also works as a soft landing gear for the SAV. Because of this design no additional landing gear is needed, and the gripper can grasp various objects with its two configurations, so the aerial grasping system is more streamlined and efficient. Our contributions are summarized below.

- Modular connectors are integrated, which reduces the time for configuring and fabricating the soft gripper fingers. With only four fingers the gripper can be arranged into two configurations, which gives a range of options for grasping target objects depending on their shapes. This modularity makes the gripper more adaptable for grasping various objects in aerial operations.

- The soft gripper can be both a grasping mechanism and a landing gear. When it is deflated it works as a soft landing gear, so an additional rigid landing gear is not needed and the weight of the SAV is reduced. This weight reduction makes flight more efficient and makes aerial operation control less complex.

- The lightweight soft gripper with a traditional quadrotor weighs only 808 g (with its H-base gripper), and it successfully grasps a cylindrical plastic container that weighs 217 g in mid-air. This payload-to-weight ratio is better than the ones in previous investigations.

steps.text:
INTRODUCTION
## I-A Motivation

Aerial grasping [1] is a rapidly growing research field, particularly for unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) used for drone delivery such as food delivery [2], search and rescue [3], environmental cleaning [4], and medical goods delivery [5]. Ensuring the safety and efficiency of goods during drone delivery is critical. We therefore aim to address these concerns with a novel solution: a soft aerial vehicle (SAV) equipped with a modular soft pneumatic gripper, which has received limited attention in previous studies.

Soft grippers offer a promising alternative to rigid grippers because of their simplified control systems, reduced complexity, and excellent force absorption. Following the principles of soft robotics, these lightweight and controllable mechanisms provide stability during grasping by dampening impact forces, and their flexibility allows a broader range of object dimensions, increasing grasping tolerance. Positioned beneath the center of gravity of the SAV, the soft gripper can inflate and deflate to grasp objects securely, improving grasping efficiency and reducing mission time. Moreover, replacing the rigid landing gear with the proposed soft gripper as the landing mechanism enhances the aerial manipulation capability of the SAV [6]. This removes the need for additional actuators and simplifies the control system, since the complicated landing gear adjustment during takeoff, landing, and grasping is no longer needed. Furthermore, the modular design of the gripper allows configuration changes for various object sizes and shapes, for instance the diverse shapes of food packages common in food delivery scenarios.

## I-B Related Work

Inspired by biological systems like birds [7], soft grippers have been shown to mitigate contact forces and compensate for grasping inaccuracies, an example of morphological computation, which combines passive mechanical components with explicit control [8]. To use these advantages, some researchers have developed a bio-inspired tendon-actuated soft gripper, as the bending of the gripper can be easily controlled by manipulating the attached tendon [9,10,11]. In the context of perching, Ramon et al. [12] designed a soft landing gear system that lets an aerial drone perch autonomously on pipes in industrial environments, providing robust attachment with nylon strands and a modular design for gripper replacement. In outdoor experiments this soft gripper closed successfully around pipes, and the quadrotor performed well even in uncertain and windy conditions despite imperfect centering or fastening. Furthermore, Fishman et al. [13,6] developed a tendon-actuated soft gripper for a soft drone inspired by the dexterity of human fingers. Their approach needs no gripper state measurement, operating the soft gripper open-loop to grasp objects of unknown shape on unknown surfaces by relying on the centroid of the objects.

Fabricating the tendon-actuated soft gripper involves inserting tubes inside the soft fingers for the tendons to pass through [14,15]. In contrast, a pneumatic soft gripper only requires a sufficient air chamber in each soft finger for bending [16]. Moreover, the location of the tendon-actuated gripper is constrained by the position of the driven motor, whereas soft pneumatic grippers offer greater configurational flexibility thanks to the flexible air tube, which can quickly connect the pneumatic soft gripper with the pumps and valves. Related work also explores pneumatic soft systems for aerial grasping. Shtarbanov [17] developed FlowIO, a wearable and modular pneumatic platform for soft robotics, which showed the viability of pneumatic systems in miniaturized applications that are cost-effective for UAVs performing aerial grasping. Ping et al. [18] integrated a soft pneumatic gripper beneath a conventional drone, similar to our design. However, their work does not explicitly focus on autonomous aerial grasping tasks or on removing the need for additional rigid landing gear. Their soft gripper is controlled by a single command, pneumatic pressure, and they claim that installing the entire Grasping Unit has minimal impact on the dynamics of the quadrotor. Since their soft gripper does not stick out by adding extra degrees of freedom (DOF) to facilitate grasping, the rigid landing gear of their UAV limits the grasping altitude. In [19], a 2 DOF robot arm with a pneumatic soft gripper is installed under a traditional UAV with rigid landing gear. Compared to our SAV, the work of Sarkar et al. [19] needs extra mechanisms and control algorithms to ensure the manipulator can reach its home and pick positions. In addition, their fixed, rigid landing gear increases the net weight of the UAV, which is over 3 kg in total.

## I-C Contribution

The proposed SAV is a significant advancement, capable of aerial grasping and landing with a lightweight modular soft pneumatic gripper. The pneumatic soft gripper, which uses a feed-forward proportional controller for precise pressure regulation, also serves as a soft landing gear for the SAV when deflated. This design eliminates the need for additional landing gear and lets the gripper grasp various objects with its two configurations, resulting in a more streamlined and efficient aerial grasping system. Our contributions are summarized as follows.

- • Integrating modular connectors reduces the configuration and fabrication time of the soft gripper fingers. With only four fingers, the gripper can be arranged into two configurations, giving a versatile range of options for grasping target objects based on their shapes. This modularity makes the gripper more adaptable to grasping various objects during aerial operations.

- • The soft gripper serves as both a grasping mechanism and a landing gear. When deflated, it functions as a soft landing gear, removing the need for an additional rigid landing gear and reducing the weight of the SAV. This weight reduction improves flight efficiency and reduces the complexity of aerial operation control.

- • The proposed lightweight soft gripper with a traditional quadrotor, weighing only 808 g (with its H-base gripper), successfully grasps a cylindrical plastic container weighing 217 g in mid-air. This payload-to-weight ratio exceeds those in previous investigations [6,18,19].
